title: The Mill and the Tower: a Piedmontese architect pours Buenos Aires in concrete
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Lanzo, Turin, and the Schools of the North

stops.name: Lanzo Torinese, birth in the valley of the Stura
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a hill town in the valleys above Turin, Luiggi Gianotti and Bernardina Monaco have a son on the fourth of April and name him Francesco Terenzio. Lanzo Torinese sits where the Stura comes down out of the mountains, in a country of stone bridges and quarry carts, and the young men of it leave. The century he is born into will send more Piedmontese across the Atlantic than any war ever sent north over the Alps, and he will be one of them. The ironwork, the glass and the mansard roofs of this province will cross with him. The birth is entered at Lanzo, in the province of Turin, in April 1881.
suggested_refs: Parish and civil birth records of Lanzo Torinese, province of Turin, April 1881

stops.name: Turin, the architect's title from the Accademia Albertina
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in any source consulted
stops.campa: He takes the title of architect from the Accademia Albertina di Belle Arti, in the street behind the Po that carries the academy's own name, and his brother Giovanni Battista takes it in the same year from the same school. Two sons of a mountain town come out of Turin holding two degrees in a profession their father did not practise. The academy has taught them drawing, ornament and the orders of classical architecture. Within a decade the elder will be working in reinforced concrete. Nobody in Turin is teaching that to anybody in 1904.
suggested_refs: Enrolment and degree registers of the Accademia Albertina di Belle Arti, Turin, 1900-1904

Alfredo Melani (1859-1928), named as Gianotti's teacher by the Italian record but professor and later director at the Scuola superiore d'arte applicata all'industria in Milan, not in Turin: the two facts are not yet reconciled

stops.name: Brussels, the postgraduate year
stops.date_confidence: year attested (single source, es.wikipedia); no address, atelier or month recorded
stops.campa: The brothers spend a postgraduate year in Brussels, the city where Victor Horta had already shown a generation what iron and glass could do inside a private house and inside a workers' hall. Gianotti walks streets where the new architecture is not a plate in a magazine but a built fact with a door handle on it. Eight years from now he will be putting curved glass and wrought iron over a shopping street eleven thousand kilometres to the southwest. Whose atelier he sat in during this year, at what address, under which master, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: Victor Horta's Hotel Tassel and Maison du Peuple, Brussels, standing and in use during Gianotti's 1905 stay
Henry van de Velde, cited by es.wikipedia as an influence on this stay although he had been based in Weimar since 1899

stops.name: Milan, pavilions for the Esposizione del Sempione
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the individual pavilions are not itemised in the sources
stops.campa: The Esposizione Internazionale del Sempione opens in Milan and Gianotti draws pavilions for it, the first commission of any size in his life. Not one of them survives the year. Exhibition architecture is built to astonish a crowd for one season and then come down, which teaches a young man plaster and speed long before it teaches him permanence, and everything he learns here about stopping a stranger in the street he will spend later on buildings meant to outlast him. He is twenty-five, working in lath and plaster on a fairground by the Sempione.
suggested_refs: Catalogue of the Esposizione Internazionale del Sempione, Milan 1906

stops.name: Genoa, the emigrant passage for the River Plate
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the 1909 arrival in Buenos Aires is attested, the port of embarkation and the ship are named in no source consulted
stops.campa: The traffic out of northern Italy for the River Plate leaves from Genoa, and in 1909 Gianotti joins it. He crosses as a qualified architect holding the degree of a royal academy, which puts him in a very small minority among the hundreds of thousands taking the same water in the same decade. Three weeks of open ocean lie between the mole under the Lanterna and the brown estuary the Spanish named for silver. He carries a portfolio of exhibition pavilions that no longer exist. The ship, the line and the date of sailing are named in no source consulted. He is twenty-eight.
suggested_refs: Passenger lists of the Genoa-Buenos Aires lines, 1909
The canonical Genoa embarkation pin used across the corpus for northern Italian crossings to the River Plate

stops.name: Buenos Aires, coming ashore at the immigrants' basin
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the dock, the ship and the day of landing are reconstructed from the period's arrival infrastructure
stops.campa: He comes ashore in a city taking in a quarter of a million people a year, through the machinery built for exactly that: the customs sheds and the immigrants' hotel on the northern basin. Within weeks he has a drawing board in the studio of Arturo Prins and Oscar Ranzenhofer, drafting other men's buildings in a professional language he is still learning to hear. The Republic is a year short of its centenary and intends to celebrate the date with architecture, which means every drawing office in the city is about to be busy. On the Prins and Ranzenhofer payroll he is one more Italian name.
suggested_refs: The Hotel de Inmigrantes, Av. Antartida Argentina 1355, Buenos Aires, receiving arrivals in 1909
The practice of Arturo Prins and Oscar Ranzenhofer, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, raising the Italian pavilion of the Centennial
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the pavilion's site within the scattered Centennial exposition is not pinned by any source consulted
stops.campa: The Centennial exposition scatters itself across the city, a section to a park, and Italy sends a pavilion designed in Milan by Gaetano Moretti and shipped in pieces to be raised on Argentine ground. Gianotti and Mario Palanti do the raising. Both are young, both out of northern Italy, and both will spend their careers giving Buenos Aires fronts that look nothing at all like the country behind the city; this is the first time they stand on the same site. The pavilion comes down when the celebration ends. Which of the exposition's scattered parks it stood in, the sources do not say.
suggested_refs: Gaetano Moretti, designer of the Italian pavilion of the Exposicion Internacional del Centenario, 1910
mario_palanti.journey.json, for Palanti's own 1909 arrival and Buenos Aires practice

stops.name: Lanzo Torinese, the season back in Italy
stops.date_confidence: single-source and unresolved: es.wikipedia records a brief return to Italy after the Centennial; en.wikipedia does not. Destination, purpose, month and duration are all unrecorded
stops.campa: After the Centennial he goes back to Italy for a season, and the record keeps only the fact of it. No city is named, no reason, no length of stay. Between the pavilion raised in Buenos Aires and the studio he will open on Paraná there is this gap, in which a man of twenty-nine settles with himself whether the rest of his life happens in Piedmont or on the estuary. He comes back. He will not see Lanzo Torinese again except as a birthplace written on a document.
suggested_refs: Italian civil and consular records for 1910-1911, unexamined

stops.name: Parana 972, the studio opens
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: He opens his own studio at Paraná 972, a few blocks north of the Congress, and stops drafting for other architects. From this address the drawings go out for the next four decades: galleries, confectioneries, apartment houses, a circus pavilion, a shipping company's palace. He works the same downtown blocks in the same years as Mario Palanti and Virginio Colombo, three Italians selling the Argentine bourgeoisie a style it has seen in European magazines and wants in stone. Colombo is the one every later account of Buenos Aires Art Nouveau will pair him with.
suggested_refs: Virginio Colombo, Italian-born Art Nouveau architect of Balvanera, Almagro and Monserrat, collaborator from 1911
mario_palanti.journey.json

stops.name: Florida 165, the competition won
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; exact day not given
stops.campa: In September the competition for a commercial gallery cutting from Florida through to San Martín is decided, and Gianotti wins it. What he has drawn is not a building of any kind Buenos Aires knows. It is a covered street with a tower on top: fourteen floors, fourteen elevators, offices, apartments, a basement theatre, the whole of it to be poured in reinforced concrete instead of raised in load-bearing brick. The estimate runs to fifteen million pesos fuertes. He is thirty-one years old and has never yet built anything intended to stand.
suggested_refs: Records of the 1912 design competition for the Galeria Guemes, Florida 165, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Rivadavia and Callao, ground broken for the Molino
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month of the start of works not given
stops.campa: Across from the National Congress, on the corner of Rivadavia and Callao, Cayetano Brenna commissions a confectionery to replace the one already trading there under the sign of the windmill. Both of his great buildings are on the boards in this same year, eight blocks apart. Gianotti draws this one and the Compañía General de Obras Públicas pours it: reinforced concrete again, an order for more than a hundred and fifty square metres of stained glass, and a mill sail set to turn on the roof above the legislators who will cross the road for their coffee.
suggested_refs: Cayetano Brenna, commissioner of the Confiteria del Molino
The Compania General de Obras Publicas, contractor

stops.name: Galeria Guemes, the first spade
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ground is broken on Florida on the tenth of March. Thirty-two months of work follow on a site hemmed between two commercial streets, concrete cast in place, a tower climbing toward eighty-seven metres, higher than anything on the block and higher than nearly anything in the country. A good part of the men on the scaffolding are Italians who crossed the same water Gianotti crossed four years before them. Argentina has no building code written for this material at this height, and the engineers are learning it on the job.
suggested_refs: Construction records of the Galeria Guemes, 1913-1915

stops.name: Salta, the central market
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a single account attributes the market to Gianotti with no drawing, contract or photograph attached; the year is not independently corroborated
stops.campa: A market hall for the city of Salta carries his name, fifteen hundred kilometres northwest of Florida Street, in the old colonial capital under the eastern cordillera. Nothing else in his catalogue stands that far from the estuary. The attribution rests on one line in one account, unaccompanied by any drawing or contract. If it holds, a practice three years old was already being called on from a province most of Buenos Aires has never seen and does not think about. Whether it holds, nothing consulted can say.
suggested_refs: Municipal building records of Salta for the central market, unexamined

stops.name: Galeria Guemes, the gallery opens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The gallery opens on the fifteenth of December, thirty-two months after the first spade. Fourteen floors, fourteen elevators, eighty-seven metres to the top of the tower, and underneath it all a passage of shops running clean through the block beneath vaulted glass. Fifteen million pesos fuertes have gone into it. Gianotti is thirty-four, and six years ago he stood at somebody else's drawing board. The Spanish record calls it the first building in the country put up entirely in reinforced concrete, and a good many people call it the first Argentine skyscraper.
stops.quote: el primer edificio de dicho pais construido enteramente en hormigon armado
suggested_refs: The mirador at the top of the Guemes tower, 87 metres above Florida
Julio Cortazar's story El otro cielo (1966) and Antoine de Saint-Exupery's residence in the building, both later engagements with this gallery

stops.name: Confiteria del Molino, the doors open
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Molino opens on the ninth of July, the national holiday, with sections of it still unfinished. Bronze handles, marble counters, ceramic tile, stained glass by the hundred square metres, and over the corner the sails of a mill turning above the traffic. Congress is across the road, and the building becomes the canteen of the Argentine political class: the presidents Uriburu, Justo and Alvear will take coffee here, and Prince Umberto of Italy, and the tenors Tito Schipa and Beniamino Gigli, and the writers Leopoldo Lugones and Roberto Arlt.
stops.quote: El edificio actual fue inaugurado el 9 de julio de 1916
suggested_refs: The stained glass and the roof mill of the Confiteria del Molino, Av. Rivadavia 1801

stops.name: Corrientes 480, the circus pavilion
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded, and the demolition date is not given
stops.campa: On Corrientes, at numbers 480 to 496, he puts up a pavilion for a circus, a building type that appears in no architectural treatise and draws very large crowds in Buenos Aires. The street is not yet the widened avenue of theatres it will become, and when the widening comes, blocks like this one go. Of the entire building there survives one line in a catalogue: an address, a year, and one capitalised word for what was done to it. The date of the demolition is nowhere recorded. It is the least documented thing he ever built.
suggested_refs: Photographic archives of Avenida Corrientes before the 1930s widening

stops.name: Parana 972, the curves go out of the drawings
stops.date_confidence: the Italian account dates the stylistic turn to about 1918; it is a periodisation, not an event
stops.campa: The curves go out of his drawings. From about this year the work turns toward what the Italian account calls an eclecticism between neoclassicism and Moorish revival: heavier cornices, symmetrical fronts, ornament fetched from further away and laid on more soberly. Art Nouveau gets perhaps eight good years in Buenos Aires and they are ending, in this city as in every other, all at once. The Italian account dates the change to about this year and gives no month for it, which makes it a periodisation and not an event. The office stays open, the clients stay, the concrete stays, and the face changes.
stops.quote: un eclettismo tra neoclassicismo e revival moreschi
suggested_refs: Comparative study of the Guemes facade (1915) and the Schaffhausen front (1932)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, marriage to Amelia Vercesi
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month, and neither church nor civil registry is named
stops.campa: He marries Amelia Vercesi. Three sons follow, Aníbal, Pedro and Juan Francisco, their birth dates unrecorded in anything that has been read. Gianotti is thirty-eight, ten years in the country, with the two buildings that will outlive him already standing eight blocks apart and full of people. He is no longer an immigrant draughtsman; he is a Buenos Aires architect with a household. Forty years on a son will be signing drawings beside him, listed as Luis Pedro, a name the sources never reconcile with the other three.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires civil marriage registers, 1919

stops.name: Posadas 1064, the Brach residence
stops.date_confidence: year attested from the published works list; month unrecorded
stops.campa: A house for the Brach family on Posadas, in the blocks under the Recoleta cemetery where Buenos Aires keeps its money and buries it. It is a private commission in a decade when his name is mostly on public-facing work, on galleries and shopfronts and offices, and it moves him inside the domestic taste of the class that had been buying the shopfronts. Posadas is a short, steep street of French roofs cut by Italian masons. He is forty-two years old when he signs the drawings.
suggested_refs: Residencia Brach, Posadas 1064, Retiro, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Roque Saenz Pena 660, the Italia-America palace
stops.date_confidence: single-source: en.wikipedia gives 1927 and the number 622; es.wikipedia gives the number 660 and no year at all. One building, two addresses, one undated
stops.campa: A palace on Avenida Roque Sáenz Peña, the cut that Buenos Aires calls the Diagonal Norte, built for the Italia-América navigation company: the emigrant passage trade, housed at last in stone at the destination end of its own route. Gianotti took that crossing himself in 1909, in the other direction and in somebody else's ship. The Spanish catalogue lists the building at number 660 and gives it no year; the English one puts it at 622 and dates it 1927. It is one building, and the record cannot agree on its number.
stops.quote: Palacio Italia America, propiedad de la Compania de Navegacion Italia-America, Av. Roque Saenz Pena 660
suggested_refs: Company records of the Italia-America navigation line, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Rosario, the flag monument competition
stops.date_confidence: contradicted: one account credits Gianotti with first prize in 1928, while the monument as built was won by Angel Guido and Alejandro Bustillo in a competition of 1939-1940 and inaugurated in 1957. Not resolved
stops.campa: One account credits him with first prize in a competition for the national flag monument at Rosario, on the bank of the Paraná. Nothing was built to his design. The monument that stands on that ground was won by Ángel Guido and Alejandro Bustillo in a later competition altogether and inaugurated thirty years after this date. Either Gianotti took an early round that came to nothing and left no drawing, or the credit is an error copied forward from one page to the next. The record as it stands does not decide.
suggested_refs: Competition records for the Monumento Historico Nacional a la Bandera, Rosario, 1928 and 1939-1940
sources: Wikipedia (ES), 'Monumento Historico Nacional a la Bandera'

stops.name: Rivadavia and Callao, the Molino damaged in the coup
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the source gives no month or day for the damage
stops.campa: The coup of 1930 puts the first military government of the Argentine twentieth century into the Casa Rosada, and the corner of Rivadavia and Callao takes damage in the disorder. The Molino stands across from a Congress that has just been dissolved. Fourteen years open, it is by now a fixture of the legislative district, and what happens to the legislature happens to its glass. The source gives no month and no day for the damage. Gianotti is forty-nine, and he will be back on his own corner within the year with a repair drawing.
suggested_refs: The Argentine coup d'etat of September 1930 and the Congress district

stops.name: Rivadavia and Callao, the Molino reopens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Repaired, the Molino reopens on the twelfth of October, a little over a year after the coup that broke it. Gianotti is fifty and has come back to a building of his own to put it back the way it was, which is not the same trade as drawing it. The confectionery goes on serving a political class whose parliament, across the road, will open and close and open again for the rest of the century. Over the corner, above the traffic on Callao, the mill sails turn again.
suggested_refs: Restoration works at the Confiteria del Molino, 1930-1931

stops.name: Reconquista 336, the Schaffhausen building
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: The Edificio Schaffhausen goes up on Reconquista, at numbers 336 to 356, in the narrow streets behind the banks. The Art Nouveau has gone out of it entirely; the front is sober, the proportions plain, the concrete poured with the same command that made the tower on Florida possible seventeen years earlier. He is fifty-one, working in a city three years into a world depression that has emptied most order books in the profession. His has not emptied. The building still stands on Reconquista.
suggested_refs: Edificio Shaffhausen, Reconquista 336/356, San Nicolas, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Mendoza, the Gran Hotel Plaza remodelled
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: He goes west to Mendoza to remodel the Gran Hotel Plaza, in the wine city at the foot of the Andes, a thousand kilometres from Florida Street. It is the second commission of his life to take him out of Buenos Aires, and the last one recorded. A remodelling is a different trade from a tower: he is fitting himself to another architect's walls, in a province where nobody has seen his gallery except in a photograph. Behind the hotel the cordillera stands. He was born under mountains on the other side of the world, and he is fifty-two.
suggested_refs: Gran Hotel Plaza, Mendoza, remodelling of 1933

stops.name: Cordoba, the marble quarry
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the quarry's location within Cordoba province is not specified, and the coordinate is the provincial capital as placeholder
stops.campa: At sixty-one he takes hold of the other end of the trade and begins working a marble quarry in the sierras of Córdoba. For thirty years he has been specifying stone by the slab on drawings. Now he is taking it out of the hill. Argentina in these years imports very little, and a domestic quarry is a business rather than an eccentricity, though there is something of the mountain town in an architect who ends up back at the rock face. The province is named in the record. The site inside it is not.
suggested_refs: Marble quarries of the Sierras de Cordoba, 1940s

stops.name: Arenales 2080, the last commission
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded
stops.campa: The last project in his catalogue is a building at Arenales 2080, in Barrio Norte, drawn and carried out with his son Luis Pedro. Fifty-five years stand between this address and the diploma taken in Turin. The architecture of 1959 is not his architecture and the son is doing much of the work, but the name on the file is still Gianotti, and the site is a dozen blocks from the studio on Paraná where the practice opened in 1911. He is seventy-eight. After this the catalogue stops.
suggested_refs: Arenales 2080, Recoleta, Buenos Aires (1959), with Luis Pedro Gianotti

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death of the architect
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Francisco Gianotti dies in Buenos Aires on the thirteenth of February, eighty-five years old, an Argentine citizen by naturalisation and a Piedmontese by birth. No funeral notice, no cemetery and no grave for him has been found in any source consulted. Behind him stand the gallery on Florida with its tower, the corner opposite Congress with the mill on the roof, and a scatter of fronts along the diagonal and the bank streets. Fifty-eight of his eighty-five years belong to Argentina.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires death registers and cemetery records for February 1967, unexamined

stops.name: Galeria Guemes, the first fire
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month or day given, and whether the fire fell before or after Gianotti's death on 13 February is not stated by any source
stops.campa: Fire takes the entrance to the first dome in the year of the architect's death. Whether he learned of it before the thirteenth of February, or whether it came after him, nothing on the record says. The gallery is fifty-two years old, its ironwork already dark with half a century of a port city's smoke, and what goes back into the burned opening is not what came out of it. The repairs that follow are not restorations, and nobody at the time calls them that.
suggested_refs: Fire damage reports, Galeria General Guemes, 1967

stops.name: Galeria Guemes, the Florida facade burns
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the tenth of September a major fire damages the Florida front. Between the two fires and the reconstruction that answers them, the original facade is substantially lost: what a pedestrian on Florida looks at after 1971 is a mid-century face fitted to a 1915 building. Inside, the passage and the vaulting and the domes come through. The building keeps its section and loses its skin, and the street-level face Gianotti was best known for is gone. He has been dead four and a half years.
suggested_refs: The fire of 10 September 1971 and the subsequent reconstruction of the Florida facade

stops.name: Galeria Guemes, the museum's citation
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the citation is an honorific of the Museo de la Ciudad, not a heritage listing
stops.campa: The Museo de la Ciudad issues a citation naming the gallery living testimony of the citizens' memory. It is an honorific from a municipal museum and not a legal protection, and it arrives at a moment when downtown Buenos Aires is losing older buildings at speed to demolition and to neglect. Seventy-two years after it opened, the covered street through the block is still a covered street through the block, with shops along it and people walking from Florida to San Martín without going outside. The citation is dated 1987 and confers nothing.
stops.quote: Testimonio vivo de la memoria ciudadana
stops.quote_source: Museo de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, 1987, cited in Wikipedia (ES), 'Galeria General Guemes'
suggested_refs: Museo de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, citations of 1987

stops.name: Rivadavia and Callao, the last uses of the Molino
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: By the middle of the nineties the Molino is a confectionery in name and a wreck in fact, its upper floors shut, its ownership passed down through hands that could not hold it. On the fourth of March a film crew works inside, shooting a music video during the production of Evita in the city. It is among the last uses the building has. The coffee goes on being served across from Congress for ten more months. The counters are still marble and the glass is still in the windows.
suggested_refs: Filming at the Confiteria del Molino, 4 March 1996

stops.name: Confiteria del Molino, the doors close
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of January the doors close. Eighty years and six months after the ninth of July 1916, the confectionery that fed the Argentine parliament stops trading and the corner goes dark. The stained glass stays in the windows, the marble stays on the counters, and the mill on the roof stops. The building is eighty years old and structurally intact and has no use at all. Deputies and senators cross Callao all week, and there is nowhere on that corner to sit down.
suggested_refs: Closure of the Confiteria del Molino, 24 January 1997

stops.name: Confiteria del Molino, National Historic Monument
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine months after it closes, the Molino is declared a National Historic Monument. The declaration protects a building that has no tenant and no owner willing to restore it, and it changes nothing about the padlock on the door. It does establish that the corner cannot legally be knocked down, which in Buenos Aires in 1997 is not a small thing to establish. By now the architect is better known by his corner than by his name. Gianotti has been dead thirty years.
suggested_refs: Declaration of the Confiteria del Molino as Monumento Historico Nacional, 24 October 1997

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the monograph
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month not given
stops.campa: CEDODAL publishes the first book given entirely to him, Francisco Gianotti. Del Art Nouveau al Racionalismo en la Argentina. The subtitle carries the whole argument: that the man who drew the ironwork on Florida Street and the man who drew the sober front on Reconquista are one architect moving with his century, not a Liberty stylist who lost his nerve at forty. The historian Horacio Eduardo Caride writes in the same rediscovery, under a title that puts the avant-garde up in the mansard roof. It is thirty-three years since he died.
stops.quote: Francisco Gianotti: la vanguardia en la mansarda
stops.quote_source: Horacio Eduardo Caride, essay title, Arquitectura en Linea
suggested_refs: CEDODAL, Francisco Gianotti. Del Art Nouveau al Racionalismo en la Argentina (Buenos Aires, 2000), ISBN 987-95996-8-3
Horacio Eduardo Caride, 'Francisco Gianotti: la vanguardia en la mansarda', Arquitectura en Linea

stops.name: Galeria Guemes, the restoration begins
stops.date_confidence: start year attested; the work runs to 2008, exact months not given
stops.campa: A full restoration begins under the architect Reinaldo Lemos and runs four years: the passage, the domes, the vaulted glass, the ironwork left by two fires and by the repairs that followed them. Eighty-nine years after it opened, the first reinforced-concrete building in Argentina is taken apart and put back by people who were not born when it burned. The shops stay open throughout. The gallery has been a working commercial street since 1915 and does not close in order to be repaired.
suggested_refs: Reinaldo Lemos, restoration of the Galeria Guemes, 2004-2008

stops.name: Galeria Guemes, the mirador reopens
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; exact day not given
stops.campa: In April the mirador opens again to the public: the viewing deck at the head of the tower, shut for decades, eighty-seven metres over Florida Street. From up there the city Gianotti stepped into in 1909 shows what became of it, in towers he never saw drawn, on a skyline his own building started. The gallery is ninety-five years old, six years out of a four-year restoration, and its architect has been dead forty-three years. Florida Street from up here is a pedestrian gully between shopfronts, the tower's shadow crossing it in the afternoon. On the pavement below, people queue for the lift.
suggested_refs: The mirador of the Galeria Guemes, reopened April 2010

stops.name: Congreso, the Molino expropriated
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twelfth of November the Chamber of Deputies votes to expropriate the Molino, taking into the hands of the state the building its own members have been looking at, shuttered, for seventeen years. Ninety-eight years after Cayetano Brenna opened the doors, the parliament that ate in the room buys the room. The declared plan is a restoration that recovers the original recipes and reopens the confectionery with a museum and a cultural centre inside it.
suggested_refs: Expropriation law for the Confiteria del Molino, Argentine Chamber of Deputies, 12 November 2014

stops.name: Rivadavia 1801, closed and not lost
stops.date_confidence: undated: the source describes the building's condition without giving a year, and the stop is placed provisionally
stops.campa: The building is not open. Restoration goes on behind the scaffolding and access is by reserved guided tour, a few dozen people at a time walking through the stained glass and the marble of a confectionery that has served no coffee since 1997. The stated aim is a working pastry shop, a museum and a cultural centre on the site, together with the recovery of the recipes that were made in the kitchens. What Gianotti drew in 1912 for a baker from Italy belongs now to the Argentine Republic, and across the road the Congress goes on sitting. No source consulted puts a year on any of this.
suggested_refs: Guided visits to the Confiteria del Molino during restoration
